name: International Rescue Committee: resettlement, asylum and integration (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the IRC's Resettlement, Asylum and Integration spending in the year to September 2025, U.S. $364.1m and Europe $23.3m (statement of functional expenses), Europe split equally over the six countries the 2025 Annual Report names (Germany, Greece, Italy, Poland, Serbia, the UK).
summary: The International Rescue Committee's Resettlement, Asylum and Integration programmes ($387m in the year to September 2025, 94% in the United States): reception, case management, cash and goods, job placement and other services for 314,000 refugees, asylum seekers and other newcomers, and immigration legal services for 16,607 clients, including 2,558 unaccompanied children. It comes to about 0.012 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.002-0.07), within the range of charityevals' other US social-service models: the help is worth its money on the site's log-income scale at newcomers' US consumption, and legal help that changes a case's outcome is valued as the income of staying instead of returning, with the risk of being killed after removal. The biggest uncertainties are how many legal outcomes the help changes and how much of the services others would have given anyway; both branches are discounted for missing data.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Services: cash, goods and paid help per person served (US$)
rows.explainer: Direct assistance and contributed goods in the accounts ÷ people served: about $270, counted at their cost (rent, furniture, cash).

rows.label: Services: share of people served who start a job through the IRC's employment services in the year
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1.5-8%): employment is one of several services; in Europe 459 placements came from 8,040 clients of economic programmes among 88,091 served (0.5% of all served); the US programmes run larger job-placement and matching-grant services for new arrivals, most of whom must work within months.

rows.label: Services: earnings brought forward by a job found with the IRC's help (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $8,000 ($3,000-15,000): about three months' earlier start at a newcomer's entry wage of about $2,500-3,000 a month; most would find work anyway, so only the months gained count.

rows.label: Services: value per person served (US$)
rows.explainer: Assistance at its cost, plus earnings brought forward by job placements averaged over everyone served. The time of caseworkers, interpreters and teachers is counted only through what it brings (assistance, jobs, the legal branch), not again at its cost.

rows.label: Services: healthy years from health and mental-health care, per person served
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.0005 (0-0.002) healthy years a person: part of the clients get help enrolling in health insurance, refugee health screening follow-up and counselling; the counselling's effect (about 0.3 SD of depression for those treated, a few percent of clients) is a few thousandths of a healthy year averaged over everyone served.

rows.label: Legal: share of clients whose case outcome changes because of the IRC's help
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-25%): in removal cases, immigrants with a lawyer win relief several times as often as those without (Eagly & Shafer 2015, University of Pennsylvania Law Review: represented detained immigrants about ten times as likely to obtain relief); unaccompanied children without a lawyer are mostly ordered removed. Most of the IRC's clients file applications (asylum, adjustment of status, work permits, family petitions) that some would win alone, so the share changed is far below the gap in removal cases.

rows.label: Legal: gain in ln(consumption) a year from staying in the destination instead of returning
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (0.8-2.5): a newcomer's consumption in the US (about $8,000-13,000 a person) against the origin's for people like them ($2,000-4,000 in Central America, Venezuela, Haiti and Afghanistan at US prices), ln(13,000 / 3,000) = 1.47.

rows.label: Legal: years the changed outcome lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 20 years (10-40): protection or a green card is for life, but some would have stayed by other routes later, return or move on.

rows.label: Legal: gain in ln(consumption) per changed case, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year of the gain, discounted.

rows.label: Legal: risk of being killed after removal, per changed case
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.8% (0.2-3%): homicide rates of 20-40 per 100,000 a year in Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala over 20 years give 0.4-0.8%, higher for people fleeing a named threat; deportees killed after return are documented (Human Rights Watch 2020, 'Deported to Danger').

rows.label: Deaths averted per person served (legal branch's, over the services' count)
rows.explainer: The legal branch's deaths averted, spread over the people_reached count so the template's row reads per person; it enters the result only through the legal branch below.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Judgment 2% (0-5%): legal clients are adults and older children.

rows.label: Share of deaths over five at 5-14
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (5-20%): unaccompanied children are mostly 13-17.

rows.label: Share of adult deaths at 15-49
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (80-97%): asylum seekers are mostly young adults.

rows.label: Value of a death averted, by the age mix (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death by age band × the life-value slider.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, services
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-0.9): the assistance is counted at its cost; the jobs brought forward have no trial of the IRC's services (studies of US resettlement agencies find early employment varies with agency and local labour markets, not a controlled effect).

rows.label: Counterfactual, services
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-80%): the federal reception money follows each arrival to whichever of the national agencies takes the case; without the IRC another agency, the state and family would provide much of the help, less well where the IRC is the only office.

rows.label: The IRC's share of all resources behind the services
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): volunteers, sponsor groups and public benefits clients are enrolled in (Convention 2); donated goods are already in the IRC's cost.

rows.label: Attribution share, services
rows.explainer: The shared attribution above.

rows.label: Share of reported reach that gets the service as intended
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-95%), both branches: the January 2025 suspension of refugee admissions and of reception funding cut services mid-case for many clients.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.95 (0.8-1.05), both branches: most of the line is paid by federal, state and local grants (the IRC helped allocate $35m in state and local budgets in 2025); a donor's dollar fills gaps the grants leave and may partly replace public money.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, services
rows.explainer: Thin: people are counted, but the jobs brought forward are judged with no evaluation of the IRC's services. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments, services
rows.formula: svc_evidence_adj * svc_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * svc_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, legal
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the representation gap is from observational court data, where represented cases may be stronger to begin with.

rows.label: Counterfactual, legal
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (50-90%): legal aid is scarce (most people in immigration court have no lawyer); some clients would find pro bono or paid help.

rows.label: The IRC's share of all resources behind the legal outcomes
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): clients' own work on their cases, pro bono partners and the courts.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, legal
rows.explainer: Thin: clients counted, the share whose outcome changes judged. Counted less by the shared slider.

rows.label: All adjustments, legal
rows.formula: legal_evidence_adj * legal_counterfactual_adj * legal_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * legal_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.
